summary: This informational document reviews the MPLS protocol suite in the context of IPv6 and identifies gaps that must be addressed before MPLS protocols and applications can run in IPv6-only networks.

eli5.summary: MPLS was built when most networks used the older addressing. This note checks which parts still need updates before a network can use only the newer kind.

questions: can mpls run on ipv6-only networks
subtitle: Identifying what's missing for MPLS to work in IPv6-only networks

tldr.problem: MPLS was designed when IPv4 was standard. As networks move to IPv6-only operation, some MPLS control-plane protocols, applications, and operational tools have gaps that prevent them from working without IPv4.
tldr.mechanism: This document systematically reviews MPLS components (data plane, control protocols like LDP and RSVP, applications like VPNs, and operational tools) to identify which ones need updates for IPv6-only networks.
tldr.outcome: Major gaps were found in label distribution, multipoint LSPs, VPN services, and operational diagnostics. Follow-on standards work is underway to close these gaps and allow MPLS to operate fully on IPv6-only networks.

today: RFC 7439 is an Informational RFC that remains valid. It identified gaps in 2015 that are still being addressed in follow-on standards work. Implementations should check the current status of drafts referenced in this document to see which gaps have been closed.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs IPv6 Support
sections.content:
MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) is a forwarding technique used in large networks to route traffic efficiently by prepending a short label to packets instead of looking up long IP addresses in routing tables. It was designed in an era when IPv4 was dominant.

As networks grow and IPv4 addresses become scarce, operators are deploying IPv6-only networks where devices have no IPv4 addresses at all. MPLS routers and servers increasingly need to operate in these IPv6-only environments. This document analyzes where MPLS breaks down without IPv4 and what needs fixing.
sections.eli5: MPLS uses short labels to forward traffic fast. It was built for IPv4 networks. As networks switch to IPv6-only, many parts of MPLS stop working properly.

sections.title: The MPLS Stack and Where Gaps Exist
sections.content:
MPLS has three main layers: the data plane (which moves labeled packets), the control plane (which sets up paths and distributes labels), applications (like VPN services), and operational tools (for monitoring and troubleshooting).

The data plane works fine in IPv6. Packets can be labeled and forwarded over IPv6 networks without problems. The trouble lies in control-plane protocols like LDP (Label Distribution Protocol), which tell routers how to label traffic. These protocols use IPv4-specific mechanisms for discovery, session setup, and next-hop resolution.
sections.eli5: MPLS has layers: data (carrying packets), control (setting up routes), apps (VPNs), and tools (checking health). The data layer works in IPv6. The control layer breaks.

sections.title: Major Gaps in Control Protocols and Applications
sections.content:
The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) has gaps in how it discovers peers, establishes sessions, and assigns next-hop addresses in IPv6-only networks. These are being fixed in ongoing work.

Multipoint LDP (for setting up one-to-many paths) inherits LDP's gaps and adds a new one: when a path crosses between IPv4-only and IPv6-only routers, the multipoint root address cannot be found.

VPN applications that carry IPv4 customer traffic over IPv6 MPLS backbones (a scenario called "4PE" or "4VPE") are not fully specified. RSVP-TE, BGP, and PCEP (path computation) protocols work well in IPv6, but VPN RFCs do not explicitly cover these mixed scenarios.

The MIB modules used to monitor and manage MPLS lack IPv6 textual conventions, particularly for identifiers and tunnel IDs.
sections.eli5: Label distribution breaks when setting up paths. Multipoint paths fail when crossing IPv4 and IPv6 regions. VPN rules don't cover IPv4 traffic over IPv6 cores. Management tools lack IPv6 descriptions.

sections.title: Operational Challenges: Diagnostics and Monitoring
sections.content:
When troubleshooting MPLS paths, operators use tools like LSP Ping (a diagnostic that traces paths and checks connectivity) and Extended ICMP (for error reporting). These tools fail in mixed IPv4/IPv6 scenarios:

If an IPv4 packet travels over an MPLS path, and a hop along the path is an IPv6-only router, that router cannot inspect the IPv4 payload or send back an IPv4 error message. The original sender never learns that the packet expired.

LSP Ping also uses IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses as a workaround to generate multiple loopback addresses for load-balancing tests; this practice does not fit in pure IPv6-only networks. Additionally, the IPv6 Router Alert option value for MPLS OAM was not defined.
sections.eli5: When checking if a path works, IPv6-only routers can't understand IPv4 packets trapped in the path. Diagnostic tools were built for IPv4, not IPv6.

sections.title: Work Underway and Remaining Tasks
sections.content:
Standards work is actively addressing the gaps identified. Updates to the Label Distribution Protocol (RFC 5036) are being developed to fully support IPv6. Similar updates are being drafted for multipoint scenarios, VPN services, and MIB modules.

However, as of this document's publication in January 2015, many fixes remain in draft form. Implementers should monitor ongoing IETF work to track when these updates are finalized. In the interim, IPv6-only MPLS deployments will need workarounds or partial features until the standards catch up.
sections.eli5: The IETF is writing fixes for these problems, but they take time. Until they are done, IPv6-only MPLS networks will have to work around the gaps.
